Student debt after graduation: two medians do not tell you what one borrower repaid

Six charts distinguish debt incidence, borrower means and medians, paid-off shares and the changing still-owing subgroup, with original Canadian survey data and a transparent invented example.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Historical National Graduates Survey estimates for the Class of 2020, interviewed three years later in 2023; table released 2 May 2025 and retrieved 25 October 2026. Scope: public postsecondary institutions, graduates living in Canada at interview, Canada by province of study (national estimates include the territories), All fields of study, Total – Gender, debt to any government or non-government source. The table excludes graduates who pursued further education between graduation and interview and respondents missing level or field. The all-level aggregate overlaps its five level categories and must not be added to them. Dollar means and medians concern the stated debtor subgroup. Graduation debtors and still-owing interview debtors are not the same denominator. All estimates are rounded; A/B/C codes are retained. No individual repayment, personal borrowing target, inflation conversion, causal comparison, statistical significance or current loan balance is inferred.

The central idea

Read who is included in each debt statistic. A graduation median and a later median among people still owing describe different groups, so their difference is not a typical person’s repayment.

01

Begin by reading the condition attached to each amount

The selected all-level estimates show CAD 18,800 median debt at graduation among graduates who owed money, and CAD 15,000 median debt at interview among those who still owed. Both are useful statistics. Subtracting them does not calculate a typical graduate’s repayment.

The first amount describes graduation debtors. The later amount excludes people who no longer owed by the interview. Those are different denominators, and the middle borrower in one distribution need not be the middle borrower in the other.

The charts use Statistics Canada Table 37-10-0255-01, selecting debt to any government or non-government source, Canada by province of study, all fields and Total – Gender. They do not treat a group estimate as an individual account balance.

02

2020 is the graduating class, while the interview came three years later

The 2023 National Graduates Survey concerns people who graduated from public postsecondary institutions in 2020. The source table used here was released on 2 May 2025. Downloading it on 25 October 2026 does not change the reference class or turn its figures into 2026 loan balances.

The table covers graduates living in Canada at interview and excludes those who pursued further education between graduation and interview. Respondents without a declared level or field are also excluded. Its national province-of-study estimates include the three territories.

Those exclusions matter when comparing a personal study path. A graduate who immediately entered another program is not represented by this table’s included population in the same way as someone who did not continue studying. The charts cannot describe every graduate’s debt experience.

03

The share who owed and the amount owed answer different questions

For all included study levels together, 47% owed education debt at graduation. This describes incidence among the included graduates, including those who owed nothing. The debt mean and median instead summarize people who had debt.

The five level-specific incidence estimates range from 32% for doctorate to 80% for professional programs. Their borrower medians range from CAD 13,500 for college to CAD 65,000 for professional programs, with the quality codes shown beside each estimate.

The scatter plot puts debt incidence on the horizontal axis and the debtor median on the vertical axis. These dimensions are related to different questions: how common a positive balance was, and how large the middle positive balance was. The overlapping All levels point is an aggregate, not an extra sixth disjoint population that can be added to the five levels.

04

A mean and a median summarize the borrower distribution differently

The all-level mean debt at graduation is CAD 25,200, above the CAD 18,800 median. The mean averages balances among the specified debtors; the median marks their distribution’s midpoint.

A difference between the two does not supply the full distribution, identify a particular borrower or set an appropriate personal borrowing limit. The grouped chart retains both measures for each level so one summary is not silently substituted for the other.

The level labels also follow the source classification. Its bachelor category includes specified below-bachelor university certificates and diplomas, while professional programs are a separate category. These are published groupings rather than a custom ranking of degree quality or future earning power.

05

The people who fully repaid leave the later debt-amount subgroup

The all-level source estimates report that 33% of graduation debtors had paid off their debt by interview. The later debt-amount estimates concern those who still owed: a mean of CAD 21,600 and a median of CAD 15,000.

The selected-level chart puts graduation amounts beside still-owing interview amounts, while its captions retain the subgroup condition. It does not label their difference as the amount repaid or the return on paying down a loan.

A proper median individual repayment would require an appropriate paired measure for the same individuals, together with a definition of what counts as repayment. Subtracting two published group medians cannot reconstruct that measure. Their difference can also be affected by who remains in the later subgroup.

06

Every borrower can repay while the still-owing median rises

The final chart is a fully invented three-person demonstration. Starting balances are CAD 10,000, CAD 20,000 and CAD 30,000. Later balances are CAD 0, CAD 19,000 and CAD 29,000. Every person reduced debt.

The starting median is CAD 20,000. Among the two people still owing, the later median is the midpoint of CAD 19,000 and CAD 29,000: CAD 24,000. That conditional median rose even though no one’s balance increased.

Include the paid-off zero and the later all-three median is CAD 19,000. Look instead at individual reductions—CAD 10,000, CAD 1,000 and CAD 1,000—and the median repayment is CAD 1,000. Changing the question changes the correct denominator and calculation. These original invented records are not survey respondents, a fitted model or a reconstruction of private borrower information.

07

Keep the source’s precision warning beside the value

The 36 selected observations retain 25 A codes, nine B codes and two C codes. In the source’s classification, A means excellent quality with a coefficient of variation at most 5%; B means very good, above 5% through 15%; C means good, above 15% through 25%.

Both professional-program medians in this slice carry C. Their point estimates remain visible with that qualification. The charts do not replace the codes with made-up error bars or treat a descriptive ordering as proof of a statistically significant difference.

All source estimates are rounded. The article performs no inflation conversion, adds no household records and estimates no current loan rate. A large difference in plotted amounts can justify a closer look at the evidence, while remaining separate from a causal claim about a program.

08

Use an actual balance and repayment schedule for the personal plan

Survey statistics provide context for education funding and debt discussions. A personal repayment plan still needs the actual loan balances, payment obligations, interest terms, support arrangements and cash available after essential expenses.

For example, dividing an independently chosen CAD 24,000 balance into 60 equal principal payments gives CAD 400 per payment before any interest, fee or program-specific adjustment. That arithmetic is a stated personal scenario; it cannot be inferred from the survey’s CAD 18,800 median.

  1. Check the class year, interview date and excluded population.
  2. Separate incidence among graduates from amounts among debtors.
  3. Retain each estimate’s quality code and subgroup condition.
  4. Use a paired individual measure when the question is individual repayment.
  5. Build the household cash schedule from actual balances and contract terms.

The source-level control changes the selected historical view and highlighted point. It never edits the official estimates or predicts how quickly a reader will repay.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Five charts use 36 published estimates from Statistics Canada’s National Graduates Survey, Class of 2020, interviewed in 2023; release dated 2 May 2025, retrieved 25 October 2026. One separate three-borrower chart is entirely invented. A/B/C quality codes remain attached to the official measures. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Statistics Canada · Table 37-10-0255-01 · Student debt at postsecondary graduation, by source of debt and province of study ↗

    Released 2 May 2025; original CSV and metadata retrieved 25 October 2026. Selects Class of 2020, Canada by province of study, All fields of study, Total – Gender, any government or non-government debt source. Six measures across five level categories and the overlapping all-level aggregate give 36 observations. Source estimate-specific A/B/C quality codes are preserved, with no missing selected values or suppressed estimates. Large-debt percentages are outside this article’s slice. Adapted from Statistics Canada, Table 37-10-0255-01. This does not constitute an endorsement by Statistics Canada of this product.

  2. Statistics Canada · National Graduates Survey · 2023 collection for the Class of 2020 ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026 for the relationship between the 2020 graduating class and the 2023 interview. Source table metadata supplies this slice’s further-study exclusion and category definitions. No confidential survey microdata is accessed or reproduced.

  3. Statistics Canada · Open Licence ↗

    Public aggregate observations are adapted with acknowledgement. The three-borrower demonstration, personal arithmetic and chart design are original teaching examples. No source population is assigned a personal repayment schedule or borrowing recommendation.
